stories.headline: Alterra Mountain Co. lays off workers weeks after receiving nearly $11 million in state and local tax incentives
stories.summary:
Alterra Mountain Co., the Denver-based ski resort operator, has cut an undisclosed number of corporate employees this week across multiple departments, including positions in Denver, remote roles, and some resort locations. The company, owned by KSL Capital Partners and headquartered at Zeppelin Station in RiNo, confirmed the layoffs in a statement but declined to specify how many workers were affected.

The cuts come less than a month after Alterra received nearly $11 million in local and state incentives intended to facilitate a headquarters relocation to Upper Downtown and a workforce expansion. The Colorado Economic Development Commission awarded the package — including a $1 million grant, $1 million loan, and up to $1.9 million in Job Growth Incentive Tax Credits — in part to prevent the company from moving its headquarters to Salt Lake City.

The performance-based tax credits are tied to Alterra creating 106 net new jobs at an average annual wage of $131,071 over eight years. State officials noted the company would need to restore any positions cut before it could begin claiming those credits. No federal WARN Act notice had been filed with the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment as of Friday morning.

stories.headline: Key Denver council member says relocating Denver Water facility to Lot M is not 'workable,' complicating Broncos stadium deal
stories.summary:
Denver City Councilwoman Jamie Torres said Thursday she does not support using Lot M, a five-acre parking lot near Empower Field at Mile High in the Sun Valley neighborhood, as a relocation site for Denver Water's emergency response facility — a move considered essential to clearing the way for a new Broncos stadium at Burnham Yard. Torres, whose district encompasses both Burnham Yard and the current stadium, said community opposition to the plan has been strong and sustained.

The emergency response facility currently sits within the proposed stadium footprint. Denver Water agreed to vacate Burnham Yard provided its ratepayers are not burdened with the cost. Most of the utility's campus is slated to move to a site in Denver's Elyria-Swansea neighborhood, but the emergency facility must remain centrally located to respond quickly to water main breaks and other urgent infrastructure needs.

Torres' position carries significant weight as one of 13 council members who would ultimately vote on any stadium deal. Broncos owner Greg Penner acknowledged this week that the 2031 stadium opening target will be difficult to meet given the unresolved issues. Denver Water CEO Alan Salazar said he still hopes Lot M can work with sufficient mitigation measures.

stories.headline: Broncos open preseason with 27-7 win over Falcons as Jarrett Stidham impresses in backup QB audition
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos defeated the Atlanta Falcons 27-7 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Friday night in their preseason opener, with backup quarterback Jarrett Stidham turning in a strong first half in the absence of starter Bo Nix. Stidham completed 9 of 15 passes for 131 yards and a touchdown, posting a passer rating of 110.7 and leading Denver to a 24-0 halftime advantage.

Stidham's first drive featured a 40-yard completion to Courtland Sutton, setting up a short touchdown run by fullback Adam Prentice. He later connected with running back Jaleel McLaughlin on a five-yard scoring pass in the second quarter. Cornerback Jahdae Barron added a 97-yard interception return for a touchdown before halftime.

Sam Ehlinger played the second half and completed 10 of 14 passes for 67 yards, though Denver managed just a field goal in the final two quarters. The game also marked the debut of new offensive coordinator Davis Webb, who took over play-calling duties after being promoted from quarterbacks coach. Head coach Sean Payton said the operation ran smoothly under Webb.

stories.headline: NCAA's new '5-in-5' eligibility rule creates roster challenges for Deion Sanders and Colorado Buffaloes
stories.summary:
The NCAA's new "5-in-5" eligibility rule, which gives athletes five years of eligibility within a five-year span based on age rather than waivers, is reshaping roster planning at the University of Colorado and programs nationwide. The rule eliminates medical hardship waivers and other extensions that had allowed some athletes to remain in college sports for six, seven, or eight years.

The change was triggered in part by a U.S. District Court in Denver ruling that made Class of 2022 high school graduates eligible for a fifth season. Three former CU players — defensive end Keaten Wade and kickers Alejandro Mata and Buck Buchanan — could potentially rejoin the Buffaloes as a result. Head coach Deion Sanders said Buchanan, CU's kickoff specialist last season, is the most likely returnee, though the team has only one scholarship spot available.

Sanders acknowledged the rule requires more precise long-term roster management, warning that accumulating players under expanded eligibility windows could "hurt you in several ways." He keeps a color-coded roster chart tracking each player's remaining eligibility and scholarship status. The 5-in-5 rule takes full effect in fall 2027 but is already influencing current rosters.

stories.headline: Denver Water backs Proposition 308 ballot initiative to redirect state sales tax revenue toward wildfire and watershed protection
stories.summary:
Denver Water has announced its support for Proposition 308, a proposed ballot initiative that would redirect a portion of state sales tax revenue generated on outdoor equipment — such as sleeping bags, hiking boots, and skis — toward wildfire mitigation and mountain watershed restoration. The endorsement is unusual for the state's largest water provider, which serves 1.5 million metro-area customers.

The measure would generate approximately $175 million annually when the state has a budget surplus, directing roughly $83 million each to Great Outdoors Colorado and the Colorado Department of Natural Resources. An additional $8.6 million would fund outdoor recreation promotion and family access programs. Because the funds would come from surplus revenue, the proposal would not create a new tax but could slightly reduce TABOR refunds in surplus years.

Denver Water General Manager Alan Salazar framed the initiative as an infrastructure need, noting that major wildfires — including the 2002 Hayman Fire — have repeatedly damaged the South Platte River Basin and forced the utility to spend tens of millions on watershed restoration. Signatures for Proposition 308 were submitted to the Colorado Secretary of State on July 27; the office has until Sept. 2 to verify whether enough valid signatures were collected to place the measure on the ballot.

stories.headline: Former AJ's Pit Bar-B-Q owner sentenced to federal prison for $2.3 million pandemic loan fraud
stories.summary:
Jared Leonard, former owner of the Denver-area restaurant AJ's Pit Bar-B-Q, was sentenced Thursday in federal court after admitting to fraudulently obtaining $2.3 million in COVID-19 pandemic relief loans and failing to pay taxes. Leonard pleaded guilty to the scheme, which involved misrepresenting information to secure federal emergency funds intended to help businesses survive pandemic-related closures.

The case is part of a broader federal crackdown on pandemic relief fraud that has led to prosecutions nationwide. Federal prosecutors have pursued numerous cases in Colorado involving fraudulent applications for Paycheck Protection Program loans and Economic Injury Disaster Loans distributed during the COVID-19 emergency.

The sentencing marks the conclusion of the criminal case against Leonard. Additional details on the length of his sentence were not immediately available in court records.

stories.headline: Denver housing market slows to steady pace in July as inventory rises and days on market lengthen
stories.summary:
Denver's residential real estate market cooled further in July, with homes sitting on the market longer and new listings pulling back in a typical summer pattern, according to the Denver Metro Association of Realtors' monthly report. Active listings rose roughly 3% from June to 13,115 homes, while the median days on market stretched to 21 days from 18 in June.

Despite slower turnover, pricing held firm. The close-to-list price ratio remained at 99%, indicating buyers are not pushing for steep discounts. Detached single-family homes stayed closer to seller's-market conditions, with a median of 17 days on market and a median sale price of $660,000, up approximately 2% year over year.

The attached home segment — condos and townhomes — told a different story, with inventory up nearly 6% year over year, closings down more than 12%, and the median price slipping to $380,000, putting that segment firmly in buyer's-market territory. At the high end, luxury sales above $1 million reached $5.8 billion in year-to-date volume, the strongest such stretch since 2022.

stories.headline: Longtime Denver developer Bill Mosher steps down as Mayor Johnston's consultant on downtown redevelopment
stories.summary:
Bill Mosher, the veteran Denver developer credited with leading the redevelopment of Union Station, is leaving his role as a consultant to Mayor Mike Johnston's office effective immediately, the city announced Friday. Johnston recruited Mosher out of semi-retirement in 2024 to serve as manager of special projects, tasking him with advancing the Burnham Yard stadium district plan and revitalizing Upper Downtown.

Mosher, a Denver native with roughly 50 years of development experience, played a central role in efforts to activate the city's Downtown Development Authority, which voters expanded in 2024 with $570 million in authorized funding. More than half of that money has been allocated, including loans for the Denver Energy Center redevelopment and the purchase of Denver Pavilions and nearby parking lots.

His consulting duties will be assumed by Chief of Staff Jenn Ridder and Deputy Chief Projects Officer Jen Welborn. Mosher will remain in his separate role as CEO of the Denver Convention Center Hotel Authority, the nonprofit behind the 1,100-room Hyatt Convention Center Hotel.

stories.headline: Lakewood selects Nederland town manager Jonathan Cain as new city manager after four-month search
stories.summary:
Lakewood announced Friday that it has chosen Jonathan Cain, currently the town manager of Nederland in Boulder County, as its new city manager following a four-month national search. Cain succeeds Kathy Hodgson, who retired after 18 years in the role — the longest tenure of any city manager in Colorado at the time of her departure.

Cain was selected from a pool of five finalists. Mayor Wendi Strom cited his ability to consider multiple perspectives, his empathy, and his detailed knowledge of issues facing Lakewood. Cain previously lived in Lakewood for a decade and pointed to local government's role in helping communities "solve hard problems with honesty, discipline and trust."

During his time in Nederland, Cain oversaw the town's acquisition and transition of Eldora Mountain Resort to municipal ownership and led recovery efforts following a downtown fire. His contract with Lakewood will be formally approved at the City Council's Aug. 24 meeting.

stories.headline: CBI issues Missing Indigenous Person Alert for 15-year-old Denver girl last seen Tuesday in Villa Park
stories.summary:
The Colorado Bureau of Investigation has activated a Missing Indigenous Person Alert for Jenavecia Blea, a 15-year-old Denver girl last seen Tuesday morning in the city's Villa Park neighborhood. According to CBI, Blea was last observed at approximately 10 a.m. on Aug. 11 walking away from the 1200 block of North Knox Court.

Blea is described as 5 feet 3 inches tall and 110 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. She has a tattoo of a butterfly with a red heart on the right side of her chest. CBI noted she is associated with the Cherokee Nation and Oglala Sioux Tribe.

Anyone who sees Blea is asked to call 911 or the Denver Police Department at 720-913-2000. The alert was issued Friday, three days after she was last seen.

stories.headline: Denver tech entrepreneur launches app allowing public to control Daniels & Fisher Tower light colors on 16th Street
stories.summary:
Denver tech entrepreneur Danny Newman has launched a public fundraising initiative that lets anyone pay to control the colored lights on the historic Daniels & Fisher Tower at 16th and Arapahoe streets in downtown Denver. Users can visit Newman's website and pay $10 to control the lights for five minutes or $200 to run the display from dusk to dawn, choosing from a variety of colors and animations.

Newman, who also owns My Brother's Bar, said the project was inspired by the Empire State Building's programmable lighting in New York. The tower's lighting system was upgraded last year, transitioning from manual changes to remote operation from anywhere in the world.

Proceeds from the project, beyond maintenance costs, benefit Historic Denver, a local preservation nonprofit. Newman serves on the organization's board. The Daniels & Fisher Tower, built in 1910, is one of downtown Denver's most recognizable landmarks.

stories.headline: Scattered storms, flash flood threat move across Denver metro and Eastern Plains
stories.summary:
Scattered showers and thunderstorms pushed across the Denver metro area and Eastern Plains Thursday evening, bringing significant rainfall to a region that has seen dry conditions in recent weeks. Forecasters warned of severe storm potential east of Interstate 25, with threats including large hail and wind gusts exceeding 60 mph.

A Flood Watch was in effect through 10 p.m. for portions of the Eastern Plains, where heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash flooding. Storms were expected to exit the state after midnight, with partly cloudy skies and patchy fog possible along the South Platte River Valley near Greeley by early Friday.

Additional rounds of heavy rain are forecast for Friday afternoon and evening, again with localized flash flooding possible. The cool, wet pattern is expected to persist through the weekend, with scattered afternoon and evening storms Saturday and Sunday and high temperatures limited to the low-to-mid 80s. A return to drier, warmer conditions is not expected until early next week.

topStory.headline: Iran Rejects Trump's Claim to Strait of Hormuz as War Enters Critical Negotiating Deadline
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he intends to declare the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States, saying the declaration would follow what he described as a U.S. victory over Iran. Speaking at a police academy in Nassau County, New York, Trump told an audience of law enforcement officials that the U.S. naval blockade of the strait was "unstoppable" and characterized the military campaign as a public service to the world.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi swiftly rejected the statement in a post on social media platform X, writing that the Strait of Hormuz "cannot be seized with a tweet, nor with an aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor through an election speech." Gharibabadi declared that the strait "has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian," and said Iran would continue to enforce its own blockade until the United States "accepts the reality of defeat and stops indulging in delusions."

The exchange comes as a 60-day negotiating window, established when the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June, is set to expire Monday. That agreement required Iran to make its "best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait, but both sides subsequently accused each other of violations and resumed hostilities before the end of June. The war between the U.S. and Iran, launched on Feb. 28 with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iranian military and infrastructure targets, has produced no clear resolution.

Traffic through the strait, which carried roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply before the conflict, has dropped sharply. Ship-tracking firm Kpler reported that only two vessels transited the waterway on Friday, with no crude oil shipments detected. A bulk carrier was struck by an unknown projectile in the strait on Friday, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre, which reported the crew was safe but that a damage assessment had not yet been completed.

The broader regional situation remains volatile. Global oil prices, while somewhat stabilized since the war's opening days, climbed again this week, with benchmark Brent crude futures on track for a weekly gain of roughly 6 percent as of Saturday. A Quinnipiac University poll from late July showed 60 percent of U.S. voters oppose military action against Iran, and media reports have raised concerns about strain on U.S. munitions stockpiles. Vice President JD Vance has been leading U.S. negotiating efforts, but no breakthrough has been reported as the Monday deadline approaches.
